analysis.one_liner: Funds a nationwide program to remove lead pipes from housing, paid for by taxing carried interest as ordinary income and halving the estate tax exemption.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in February 2021, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have spent up to $9.5 billion a year, for ten years, on HUD grants to find and remove lead pipes and taps in housing, would have required lead-hazard inspections and abatement in federally assisted housing, and would have required sellers and landlords to disclose lead pipe hazards to buyers and renters, with civil penalties and triple damages for knowingly hiding them. To pay for it, the bill taxed carried interest — the profit share paid to private equity and hedge fund partners — as ordinary income instead of at the lower capital-gains rate, and it cut the estate tax exemption from $10 million back to $5 million. It never got past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and buyers of older homes, especially low-income families in federally assisted housing and families with young children, who face the greatest risk of lead poisoning from old pipes and taps. Communities with aging housing stock would get federal grants for testing, temporary relocation during work, and permanent pipe removal. Workers who do lead abatement would get federally certified training.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families in older homes with lead pipes

how_it_helps.text: HUD would issue grants to state and local governments to perform risk assessments, interim controls, and full abatement of lead-based pipe hazards in priority (affordable) housing, with a 10% local match and no more than 10% for administration.
The bill authorizes $9.5 billion per year for fiscal years 2022 through 2031 for lead hazard reduction grants, plus EPA funding for lead exposure reduction.

HUD must require risk assessments, inspections, interim controls, and abatement of lead-based pipe hazards in federally assisted housing, with an initial risk assessment covering at least 50% of units within 5 years and the rest within 10 years.

Sellers and landlords would have to disclose known lead pipes and hazards, provide a hazard information pamphlet, and give buyers a 10-day window for an inspection; knowing violators face civil penalties and liability for three times the buyer's damages.
EPA must set training and certification standards so that all lead pipe risk assessment, inspection, and abatement work is done by certified contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity and hedge fund partners, who would pay ordinary income tax rates — up to 37% rather than the 20% capital-gains rate — on carried interest, and the wealthiest estates, whose tax-free exemption would drop from $10 million to $5 million. Landlords, sellers, and federally assisted housing owners would bear new inspection, abatement, and disclosure duties, though some costs could be passed through rent adjustments or covered by the new grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity partners, hedge funds, large estates

drawbacks.text: The mandate that federally assisted housing units be inspected and abated on a fixed schedule imposes real compliance costs on housing providers; the bill lets Section 8 rents be adjusted to cover abatement costs, which would flow through federal housing spending.

Sellers and landlords face civil money penalties and liability for three times the buyer's damages for failing to disclose known lead hazards, which an honest supporter would acknowledge adds legal risk and transaction friction to home sales and rentals of pre-1986 housing.

The bill's spending is authorized for ten years but depends on annual appropriations, and the revenue provisions are a permanent structural tax increase on a specific industry, so opponents would argue the tax change outlives the lead problem.

Lead pipe removal in private, non-subsidized housing is voluntary on the owner's part and funded through grants with only a 10% match, so the bill's reach into the much larger private stock depends on state and local governments choosing to apply and on annual funding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core case is strong: childhood lead exposure causes permanent neurological damage, and the bill directly funds removal while concentrating the cost on a narrow group of very high-income finance partners rather than on taxpayers broadly or on the families most exposed. The real counterweights are the compliance burden on landlords and sellers of older housing and the possibility that some abatement costs flow into rents; the bill partly offsets those with grants and rent adjustments. On balance the benefits are targeted at a serious, well-documented health hazard and the costs fall on those best able to bear them.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees in February 2021 and one subcommittee the next day, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Ryan introduced the GET THE LEAD OUT Act of 2021 on February 25, 2021, joined by Rep. Michael F. Doyle as cosponsor.

The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Ways and Means Committees, splitting jurisdiction across three committees, which is a demanding path for any bill.
On February 26, 2021, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change.
No further action of any kind appears in the record through January 3, 2023, when the 117th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity and hedge fund partners kept paying the lower capital-gains rate on carried interest, large estates kept the higher $10 million exemption, and landlords and sellers of older housing avoided the new disclosure, inspection, and abatement requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers, large estates, and landlords

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded. Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were House Democrats, and with no hearing or markup the bill never drew public support or opposition from either party at large.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: The bill would tax their carried-interest compensation as ordinary income, up to 37% instead of the 20% capital-gains rate, to finance the lead hazard program. Their interest in keeping the lower rate is directly the revenue the public program would have used.
The bill halves the estate tax exemption from $10 million to $5 million, returning it to its pre-2018 level, raising tax on large inherited estates to help fund lead removal.

industries.industry: Landlords and sellers of older housing
industries.note: They would face mandatory disclosure, inspection, and abatement duties with civil penalties and triple damages for concealment, but grant funds, Section 8 rent adjustments, and a task force on liability insurance and safe-harbor standards would offset some costs and reduce liability uncertainty.

industries.industry: Lead abatement, testing, and pipe replacement contractors
industries.note: $9.5 billion a year in grants and a certified-contractor requirement would create a decade of funded demand for lead hazard evaluation and removal work, with new EPA training and certification standards for the workforce.
